@graph.name: Local & Regional Move Operations
@graph.description: Local and regional move operations from survey to walkthrough. The operation chain runs survey, quote, pack, load, transport, unload, place, reassemble, unpack, and a final walkthrough. Survey runs through the quote form — Short (Quick Quote) default and Detailed Project, switching in place with the From, To and What's moving inputs preserved — or through the free film-only video walkthrough survey room, where the customer films and a person makes the estimate; nothing is auto-priced. The published scope is homes and businesses across the Shenandoah Valley and the Eastern Panhandle: packing and unpacking, loading and unloading, priced by the job, not by the hour, at one flat rate agreed in writing before move day. Load order runs heavy pieces low and first, room-staged boxes next, fragile items secured on top, everything strapped; placement is room by room by label, with reassembly of standard furniture. Transport follows the I-81, I-66 and I-70 corridors as the route fits. Both bases dispatch across the region — Winchester serves the Valley side, Martinsburg the Eastern Panhandle side, with overlap at Moorefield — and the quote form settles which crew and route fit the move. Where a move includes a high-mass piece of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, that item moves under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation with the KIM-GS Protocol and L/360 floor-deflection analysis, as part of the same flat-rate move. Home depth cross-references the residential category, business depth the office category, and moves beyond the region the long-distance category — cross-references are links, never duplicated claims.

process.name: Survey
process.text: The goods are surveyed — on site or on the information the customer furnishes — so the scope, access, and heavy items are known before any price exists.

process.name: Written flat-rate quote
process.text: The whole job — scope, distance, manpower, equipment — is reviewed and priced at one flat rate in writing before work begins. Hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it.

process.name: Prep and pack
process.text: Furniture is padded and wrapped; packing is done by the crew or the customer, per the quote.

process.name: Load
process.text: The load is built for the run: weight placed for the corridor drive, heavy items secured first, access constraints at both ends worked as planned at the survey.

process.name: The run
process.text: Local runs stay inside the town pair; regional runs ride I-81, I-66, or I-70 with corridor timing treated as a scheduling variable.

process.name: Placement
process.text: Items are placed in the rooms the customer names, not left at the door.

process.name: If something goes wrong
process.text: A written claim path stands behind every move — in Virginia, acknowledgment within 30 days and a decision or firm offer within 120 (§46.2-2168); the federal and West Virginia paths apply on their own moves.

@graph.name: Commercial Terms & Cost Drivers
@graph.description: Commercial terms and cost drivers for local and regional moves. The company's only pricing term is the published one: a flat rate quoted in writing before move day, priced by the job, not by the hour — hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it — under the standing promise Guaranteed Flat Rate or Your Move is Free! No company price, minimum, deposit, discount, fee, or surcharge is stated anywhere in this dataset. Every figure below is industry market data, researched and labeled as such, never a company term: local moves are priced by the hour in the market, typically a crew rate around $100 an hour for a two-person crew, often with two-to-four-hour minimums, plus travel and truck fees and extras; market totals in published guides run roughly $400 to $750 for a studio or one-bedroom home, $850 to $1,750 for two-to-three bedrooms, and $1,700 to $3,400 for four-plus bedrooms. The pricing models in the market: hourly (crew times hours, where the customer pays for every slow elevator, parking hunt, and delay), binding estimates (a fixed total for a listed scope and inventory), and flat-fee pricing (one guaranteed price set in advance from inventory, access, and distance). Under a flat or binding price the mover assumes the timing risk once the scope is locked; under hourly pricing the customer carries it. Cost drivers: inventory size, packing level, access — stairs, elevator, long carry — distance, and specialty items priced as separate line items. Booking windows in market guides: local moves book 2 to 4 weeks out off-peak and 4 to 8 weeks out in peak season, May through September with June busiest and month-ends and weekends tightest. The fear the flat rate answers is the hourly meter on a short local move; the company answer is one price in writing before the truck is loaded.

Trigger events: lease end, a home closing, a job transfer, household growth, household shrinkage, school-calendar timing, and a business premises change. Seasonality is industry research, labeled as such: peak season runs May through September, June is the most common moving month — one market dataset puts 41 percent of US moves in May through August — and month-end dates and weekends are the tightest; market guides put local booking windows at 2 to 4 weeks off-peak and 4 to 8 weeks in peak season. No availability promise is made anywhere in this dataset: the published branch hours are the hours, in every season. Search behavior from the company's own Search Console record: near-me intent is shared across the local and residential categories and converts fastest — 'movers near me' holds 246 impressions at position 5.0 with 11 clicks, the site's best click source — and Winchester-cluster searchers compare on price certainty and local presence. Every persona plans through the same quote path: the Short or Detailed quote form, or the film-only video walkthrough survey room with a human-made estimate.

researchClaims.fact: A household goods carrier may not engage in intrastate operations on any Virginia highway without first obtaining a certificate of fitness from the Department (Virginia DMV, Motor Carrier Services) — Va. Code §46.2-2150. Carriers transporting household goods less than thirty-one road miles are exempt from most of Article 4 of Chapter 21 — but not from the claims section, §46.2-2168, which applies to them anyway (§46.2-2149).
researchClaims.headline: Virginia: certificate of fitness, and the 31-road-mile line
researchClaims.scope: Virginia intrastate household-goods carriage; section texts read in full on LIS 2026-11-05.

researchClaims.fact: Every Virginia household goods carrier must file its tariffs — all rates and charges — with the Department at least thirty days before the effective date and make them available for public inspection (§46.2-2169). Charging or collecting more than the published tariff is unlawful (§46.2-2170), and the Department approves the rates and charges filed (§46.2-2155). Tariffs must separately state each accessorial service and its charge, including packing/unpacking per container or per hundredweight, and may establish an hourly labor charge for miscellaneous labor (§46.2-2173).
researchClaims.headline: Virginia: a tariff state — published rates are the legal price
researchClaims.scope: The statute controls what a carrier may charge for Virginia intrastate carriage; it sets no dollar figure itself.

researchClaims.fact: A Virginia estimate may be given only after a visual inspection of the goods by the estimator, or on information the shipper furnishes; a written estimate must be headed, in bold type, "ESTIMATED COST OF SERVICES" and carry the statutory notice that it is not a guarantee — but the carrier may bind the estimate and guarantee charges will not exceed it, except for destination accessorial tariff charges unknown until a sight survey at delivery (§46.2-2157). Section 46.2-2161(C) states the same bound/fixed rule. When a written estimate is given, the carrier must also hand the shipper a Department-approved information booklet and obtain a receipt for it (§46.2-2157(B)).
researchClaims.headline: Virginia: written-estimate rules, and the bound (flat) estimate
researchClaims.scope: This is the Virginia-law basis on which a guaranteed flat rate rests for intrastate moves — distinct from the federal binding-estimate rule (49 CFR 375.403).

researchClaims.fact: A Virginia household goods carrier that receives a written loss-or-damage claim must acknowledge it in writing within thirty calendar days and must pay, decline, or make a firm compromise settlement offer in writing within 120 days; if the claim is still pending after 120 days, the carrier must advise the claimant in writing of its status at 120 days and every thirty days after. No contract may shorten the claim-filing period below thirty calendar days or the suit period below two years (§46.2-2168).
researchClaims.headline: Virginia: the claims clock
researchClaims.scope: Applies even to the under-31-road-mile carriers exempt from the rest of Article 4 (§46.2-2149).

researchClaims.fact: Where charges turn on weight, Virginia requires tare and gross weights taken on certified scales by a certified weighmaster, with the shipper entitled to observe the weighing; the net weight goes on the bill of lading (§46.2-2163). If no certified scale is available, a constructive weight of seven pounds per cubic foot of properly loaded van space may be used (§46.2-2164). Before delivery, the shipper may demand a reweigh, and the lower of the two net weights determines the charges (§46.2-2167). Section 46.2-2101(C) sets the minimum public financial responsibility for certificated household goods carriers at $750,000, and DMV application form OA 142 requires Form E (liability) and Form H (cargo) insurance filings for household-goods authority over 30 miles.
researchClaims.headline: Virginia: weights are certified, observable, and re-weighable
researchClaims.scope: Sections read in full on LIS 2026-11-05; OA 142 read at dmv.am.virginia.gov.

researchClaims.fact: Beyond the certificate itself, the West Virginia PSC is vested with power "to fix, alter, regulate, and determine just, fair, reasonable, and sufficient rates" and to regulate the service and safety of operations of common carriers by motor vehicle (W. Va. Code §24A-2-3). The PSC's motor carrier rules — 150 CSR 9, "Rules Governing Motor Carriers, Private Commercial Carriers, and the Filing of Evidence of Insurance and Financial Responsibility by Motor Carriers" (current version effective January 13, 2022) — govern carriers' insurance and financial-responsibility filings with the Commission.
researchClaims.headline: West Virginia: PSC authority reaches rates and insurance, not just the certificate
researchClaims.scope: Claims only the certificate, rate, and insurance-filing layers verified here; §24A-1-3 exemptions were not relied on for any scope sentence.

researchClaims.fact: FMCSA states that interstate movers must be registered with the federal government and hold a U.S. DOT number, while "Local moving companies performing moves within a state are regulated by state and local laws" — and directs consumers moving within one state to their state consumer affairs agency or state moving association, since "Each state has its own rules and regulations for moving household goods within the state." The federal household-goods rulebook (49 CFR Part 375) attaches only when a move crosses a state line. Practical consequence for this footprint: a Winchester-to-Martinsburg move is an interstate (federal) move even though it is a short regional run, while Winchester-to-Front Royal is Virginia-intrastate and Martinsburg-to-Inwood is WV-intrastate — three rulebooks inside one service area.
researchClaims.headline: The federal/state split, in FMCSA's own words
researchClaims.scope: Quoted sentences verbatim from the FMCSA FAQ (Protect Your Move program), read 2026-11-05.

researchClaims.fact: The Revised NIOSH Lifting Equation sets its load constant at 51 pounds — the recommended weight limit for a lift under ideal conditions (load close to the body, at about waist height, short vertical travel, no twisting, infrequent, good grip). Six multipliers (horizontal distance, vertical position, travel distance, asymmetry, frequency, coupling) only ever reduce that limit for real tasks, which is why stairs, reach, and repetition push a one-person lift out of the safe band quickly. OSHA's materials-handling guidance is the operational companion: limit manual lifts to no more than about 50 pounds; for loads over 50 pounds use two or more people or mechanical means — hand trucks, dollies, and ramps or lift gates rather than lifting into the truck.
researchClaims.headline: Crew sizing rests on a measured limit: 51 lb, ideal conditions only
researchClaims.scope: 51 lb is an ideal-conditions ceiling for a single two-handed lift, not a per-item moving limit; OSHA companion guidance at osha.gov/etools/electrical-contractors/materials-handling/heavy.

researchClaims.fact: VDOT's I-81 Corridor Improvement Plan Final Report (January 2026) records that trucks traveling I-81 accumulate over 40 percent of all interstate truck vehicle-miles traveled statewide, transporting over $300 billion in goods annually along the 325-mile corridor; over the past six years the corridor averaged about 2,750 vehicle crashes per year, approximately one-third involving heavy trucks; and as of November 2025, 78 percent of the corridor is two lanes in each direction, so a single blocked lane cuts capacity sharply. For regional dispatch, corridor timing is a real scheduling variable, not background color.
researchClaims.headline: The I-81 operating environment (VDOT)
researchClaims.scope: All figures are corridor-wide (all 325 Virginia miles), not a Shenandoah Valley segment figure.

@graph.name: Local & Regional — Jurisdiction Boundaries
@graph.description: The scope boundaries of the local and regional category stated as data: three rulebooks operate inside one service area. A move that stays inside Virginia is Virginia-intrastate (DMV certificate of fitness, filed tariffs, the bound-estimate rule, the 30/120-day claims clock). A move that stays inside West Virginia is WV-intrastate (PSC certificate, PSC rate regulation, 150 CSR 9 insurance filings). Any move that crosses a state line — including the short Winchester-to-Martinsburg run — is interstate and federal (49 CFR Part 375), performed by contractors holding their own operating authority.

boundaries.basis: Certificate of fitness (§46.2-2150); filed tariffs are the legal price (§§46.2-2169, 46.2-2170); bound written estimates permitted (§46.2-2157); claims clock 30/120 days (§46.2-2168). Moves under 31 road miles are exempt from most of Article 4 except the claims section (§46.2-2149).
Certificate of convenience and necessity (§24A-2-5); PSC rate and service regulation (§24A-2-3); insurance and financial-responsibility filings under 150 CSR 9.

boundaries.basis: Federal household-goods rules, 49 CFR Part 375: written estimates after survey, binding vs non-binding, Full Value Protection vs Released Value (see pool entry L2-HHG-01). Interstate work is performed by contractors holding their own operating authority.
